instructions: Use black ink or ball-point pen.
If you use pencil for diagrams, sketches or graphs it must be dark (HB or B).
Fill in the boxes at the top of this page with your name, centre number and candidate number.
Answer the questions in the spaces provided; there may be more space than you need.
information: The total mark for this paper is 70.
The marks for each question are shown in brackets; use them as a guide to how much time to spend on each question.
advice: Read each question carefully before you start to answer it.
Check your answers if you have time at the end.

sections.instructions: Some questions must be answered with a cross in a box. If you change your mind, put a line through the box and then mark your new answer with a cross.

qtypes.label: Multiple choice
qtypes.description: Four options A-D, one correct answer, marked with a cross in a box.

qtypes.label: State / name / give
qtypes.description: Short factual recall: name a structure, state a function, give a definition.

qtypes.label: Describe
qtypes.description: Give an account of a process, structure or trend without needing reasons.

qtypes.label: Explain
qtypes.description: Give reasons: link a feature or change to its biological cause or effect.

qtypes.label: Calculation
qtypes.description: Magnification, percentage change, rates, means, ratios, energy efficiency, estimates.

qtypes.label: Genetic crosses
qtypes.description: Genetic diagrams, Punnett squares, ratios, probabilities and family pedigrees.

qtypes.label: Practical and experimental design
qtypes.description: Variables, controls, method, safety and reliability; six-mark plan-an-investigation questions.

qtypes.label: Data and graph analysis
qtypes.description: Read and interpret tables and graphs, describe trends, plot graphs, draw conclusions.

qtypes.label: Diagram labelling
qtypes.description: Identify and name labelled structures on a drawing and give their functions.

qtypes.label: Extended response
qtypes.description: Six-mark open response, point-marked: any six creditable points from a list (max 6).

qtypes.label: Article comprehension
qtypes.description: Paper 2 Question 1: an article with numbered lines, answered from the passage and own knowledge across the specification.

topics.title: The nature and variety of living organisms

subtopics.title: Characteristics of living organisms
subtopics.summary: The life processes that every living thing carries out.

points.summary: All living things need nutrition, respire, excrete, respond, move, control their internal conditions, reproduce, and grow and develop.

subtopics.title: Variety of living organisms
subtopics.summary: Key features of plants, animals, fungi, protoctists, bacteria and viruses, and what a pathogen is.

points.summary: Recognise the shared features of the four eukaryote groups (plants, animals, fungi, protoctists) with named examples.
Recognise the features of prokaryotes such as bacteria, with named examples.
A pathogen is anything that causes disease; it can be a fungus, bacterium, protoctist or virus; viruses are non-living particles.

topics.title: Structures and functions in living organisms

subtopics.title: Levels of organisation and cell structure
subtopics.summary: From organelles to systems; what each cell structure does; plant versus animal cells; specialised cells and stem cells.

points.summary: Living things are organised as organelles, cells, tissues, organs and organ systems.
Recognise nucleus, cytoplasm, membrane, wall, mitochondria, chloroplasts, ribosomes and vacuole.
State what each of those cell structures does.
Compare the structures found in plant cells and animal cells.
Explain why cells becoming specialised matters as an organism develops.
Weigh up the benefits and drawbacks of using stem cells in medicine.

subtopics.title: Biological molecules and enzymes
subtopics.summary: Elements and building blocks of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, food tests, and how temperature and pH affect enzymes.

points.summary: Name the elements found in carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.
Large food molecules are built from small units: sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.
Practical: test foods for glucose, starch, protein and fat.
Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up metabolic reactions.
Temperature changes enzyme activity, and high temperatures change the shape of the active site.
Practical: investigate the effect of temperature on enzyme activity.
pH affects enzyme function by changing the active site.
Practical: investigate the effect of pH on enzyme activity.

subtopics.title: Movement of substances into and out of cells
subtopics.summary: Diffusion, osmosis and active transport and the factors that change their rates.

points.summary: Describe diffusion, osmosis and active transport as ways substances cross cell membranes.
Surface area to volume ratio, distance, temperature and concentration gradient change the rate of movement.
Practical: investigate diffusion and osmosis in living and non-living systems.

subtopics.title: Nutrition in flowering plants
subtopics.summary: Photosynthesis, its equations and limiting factors, leaf structure, mineral ions and photosynthesis practicals.

points.summary: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.
Write the word and balanced symbol equations for photosynthesis.
Carbon dioxide concentration, light intensity and temperature change the rate of photosynthesis.
Describe leaf structure and explain how it suits photosynthesis.
Plants need mineral ions: magnesium for chlorophyll and nitrate for amino acids.
Practical: show oxygen release by a water plant, starch production and the need for light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll.

subtopics.title: Human nutrition and digestion
subtopics.summary: Balanced diet, nutrient sources and roles, energy needs, the alimentary canal, enzymes, bile and absorption.

points.summary: A balanced diet has the right proportions of each food group, water and fibre.
Sources and functions of carbohydrate, protein, lipid, vitamins A, C and D, calcium, iron, water and fibre.
Energy needs depend on activity, age and pregnancy.
Structure and function of the parts of the alimentary canal and the pancreas.
Peristalsis moves food along the gut.
Amylase and maltase digest starch, proteases digest protein and lipases digest lipids.
Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
Bile neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats.
The small intestine, including its villi, is adapted for absorption.
Practical: find the energy content of a food by burning it.

subtopics.title: Respiration
subtopics.summary: ATP, aerobic versus anaerobic respiration, the equations and respiring-organism practicals.

points.summary: Respiration releases energy and makes ATP.
ATP supplies energy to cells.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
Word and balanced symbol equations for aerobic respiration.
Word equations for anaerobic respiration in animals and in plants or yeast.
Practical: show carbon dioxide and heat released by respiring seeds or other organisms.

subtopics.title: Gas exchange in flowering plants
subtopics.summary: How leaves exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide by diffusion, stomata, and net exchange in light and dark.

points.summary: Gas exchange in plants happens by diffusion.
Link oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange to respiration and photosynthesis.
How leaf structure suits gas exchange.
Stomata let gases in and out of the leaf.
Respiration never stops, but the net gas exchange depends on light intensity.
Practical: use hydrogencarbonate indicator to show how light affects net gas exchange.

subtopics.title: Gas exchange in humans
subtopics.summary: Structure of the thorax, ventilation, alveoli, the effects of smoking and breathing practicals.

points.summary: Structures of the thorax: ribs, intercostal muscles, diaphragm, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, pleural membranes.
How the intercostal muscles and diaphragm ventilate the lungs.
How alveoli are adapted for diffusion of gases between air and blood.
Effects of smoking on the lungs and circulation, including coronary heart disease.
Practical: investigate breathing, carbon dioxide release and the effect of exercise.

subtopics.title: Transport in flowering plants
subtopics.summary: Why transport systems are needed, xylem and phloem, root hair cells and transpiration.

points.summary: Small single-celled organisms can rely on diffusion alone.
Large multicellular organisms need a transport system.
Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids around the plant.
Xylem carries water and mineral ions up from the roots.
How root hair cells absorb water.
Transpiration is evaporation of water from the plant surface.
Humidity, wind speed, temperature and light intensity change the rate of transpiration.
Practical: investigate environmental factors and the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot.

subtopics.title: Blood and immunity
subtopics.summary: Blood components, plasma transport, red cell adaptations, white cells, vaccination and clotting.

points.summary: Blood is red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
Plasma carries carbon dioxide, digested food, urea, hormones and heat.
Red blood cells are adapted for carrying oxygen.
Phagocytes engulf pathogens and lymphocytes make specific antibodies.
Vaccination produces memory cells, so later antibody production is quicker and larger.
Platelets help clot blood, preventing blood loss and infection.

subtopics.title: The heart and circulation
subtopics.summary: Structure of the heart, heart rate, coronary heart disease, blood vessels and the circulation plan.

points.summary: Structure of the heart and how it pumps blood.
Heart rate rises during exercise and with adrenaline.
Risk factors for coronary heart disease.
Structure of arteries, veins and capillaries related to their functions.
Plan of the circulation, including vessels serving heart, lungs, liver and kidneys.

subtopics.title: Excretion
subtopics.summary: Waste gases in plants, excretory organs, and how the kidney filters blood and controls water.

points.summary: Carbon dioxide and oxygen are metabolic wastes leaving a leaf through stomata.
Excretory products of the lungs, kidneys and skin.
The kidney excretes waste and controls body water (osmoregulation).
Structure of the urinary system.
Structure of a nephron.
Ultrafiltration in the Bowman's capsule and what the filtrate contains.
Water is reabsorbed from the collecting duct.
Glucose is selectively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
ADH controls the water content of the blood.
Urine is water, urea and ions.

subtopics.title: Co-ordination and response in plants
subtopics.summary: Stimulus-receptor-effector, homeostasis basics, tropisms and the role of auxin.

points.summary: Organisms respond to changes in their surroundings.
A co-ordinated response needs a stimulus, a receptor and an effector.
Plants respond to stimuli.
Roots and shoots show geotropism and phototropism.
Auxin causes the phototropic response of shoots.

subtopics.title: The nervous system and the eye
subtopics.summary: Nervous and hormonal control compared, the CNS, synapses, reflex arcs and the eye.

points.summary: Compare nervous and hormonal control of responses.
The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, linked to sense organs by nerves.
Receptors send electrical impulses along nerves, giving rapid responses.
Neurotransmitters carry the signal across synapses.
Structure and function of a simple reflex arc.
Structure and function of the eye.
How the eye focuses on near and far objects and responds to light intensity.

subtopics.title: Homeostasis and hormones
subtopics.summary: Keeping internal conditions constant, temperature control by the skin and the main human hormones.

points.summary: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment constant, for example water content and temperature.
How the skin controls body temperature by sweating, vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
Sources, roles and effects of adrenaline, insulin, testosterone, progesterone and oestrogen.
Sources, roles and effects of ADH, FSH and LH.

subtopics.title: Reproduction in flowering plants
subtopics.summary: Sexual versus asexual reproduction, fertilisation, flowers and pollination, germination and asexual methods.

points.summary: Differences between sexual and asexual reproduction.
Fertilisation is fusion of gametes to make a zygote that divides into an embryo.
Structures of insect- and wind-pollinated flowers and how each suits pollination.
Pollen tube growth and fertilisation lead to seeds and fruit.
Practical: find the conditions seeds need to germinate.
Germinating seeds use stored food until they can photosynthesise.
Plants reproduce asexually naturally (runners) and artificially (cuttings).

subtopics.title: Human reproduction
subtopics.summary: Reproductive systems, the menstrual cycle hormones, the placenta, amniotic fluid and puberty.

points.summary: How the male and female reproductive systems are adapted for their functions.
Oestrogen and progesterone in the menstrual cycle.
FSH and LH in the menstrual cycle.
The placenta supplies the embryo with nutrients.
Amniotic fluid protects the developing embryo.
Oestrogen and testosterone cause secondary sexual characteristics.

subtopics.title: DNA, genes and protein synthesis
subtopics.summary: Genome, genes and chromosomes, DNA and RNA structure, transcription and translation.

points.summary: The genome is all of an organism's DNA; a gene is a length of DNA coding for one protein.
Genes are found on chromosomes in the nucleus.
DNA is a double helix of two strands joined by base pairs A-T and C-G.
RNA is single stranded and has uracil in place of thymine.
Protein synthesis: transcription and translation using mRNA, ribosomes, tRNA, codons and anticodons.

subtopics.title: Monohybrid inheritance
subtopics.summary: Alleles and genetic terms, codominance, genetic diagrams, pedigrees, probabilities and sex determination.

points.summary: Alleles are different forms of a gene that cause inherited differences.
Meaning of dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, phenotype and genotype.
Meaning of codominance.
Most features are controlled by many genes (polygenic).
Use genetic diagrams to show monohybrid inheritance.
Interpret family pedigrees.
Predict probabilities from monohybrid crosses.
Sex is set by one pair of chromosomes: XX female, XY male.
Show sex determination at fertilisation with a genetic diagram.

subtopics.title: Cell division, variation and mutation
subtopics.summary: Mitosis and meiosis, chromosome numbers, causes of variation and how mutations arise and act.

points.summary: Mitosis of a diploid cell gives two genetically identical cells.
Mitosis happens in growth, repair, cloning and asexual reproduction.
Meiosis gives four genetically different haploid gametes.
Random fertilisation adds genetic variation.
Human body cells have 46 chromosomes and gametes have 23.
Variation can be genetic, environmental or both.
A mutation is a rare, random change to genetic material that can be inherited.
A DNA change can alter the amino acid sequence and so the phenotype.
Most mutations have no effect, some a small effect and very few a large effect.
Ionising radiation and some chemicals increase the mutation rate.

subtopics.title: Natural selection and antibiotic resistance
subtopics.summary: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection and how antibiotic resistance spreads.

points.summary: Explain evolution by natural selection.
How antibiotic resistance increases in bacteria and why that makes infections hard to treat.

subtopics.title: The organism in the environment
subtopics.summary: Ecological terms, quadrat sampling, biodiversity and how abiotic and biotic factors affect populations.

points.summary: Meaning of population, community, habitat and ecosystem.
Practical: use quadrats to compare a population in two areas.
Meaning of biodiversity.
Practical: use quadrats to study distribution and measure biodiversity.
Abiotic and biotic factors change population size and distribution.

subtopics.title: Feeding relationships
subtopics.summary: Trophic levels, food chains and webs, ecological pyramids and energy transfer between levels.

points.summary: Names of trophic levels: producers, primary, secondary and tertiary consumers, decomposers.
Food chains, food webs and pyramids of number, biomass and energy.
Energy and materials pass along food chains.
Why only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next.

subtopics.title: Cycles within ecosystems
subtopics.summary: The carbon cycle and the nitrogen cycle and the organisms that drive them.

points.summary: Stages of the carbon cycle: respiration, photosynthesis, decomposition and combustion.
Stages of the nitrogen cycle and the roles of fixing, decomposing, nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria.

subtopics.title: Human influences on the environment
subtopics.summary: Air pollution, greenhouse gases and global warming, sewage, eutrophication and deforestation.

points.summary: Biological effects of sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide pollution.
Water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, methane and CFCs are greenhouse gases.
Human activities that release greenhouse gases.
More greenhouse gases cause an enhanced greenhouse effect, global warming and its effects.
Biological effects of sewage in water.
Eutrophication caused by fertiliser leaching and its consequences.
Effects of deforestation on soil, water cycle, carbon cycle and atmospheric gases.

subtopics.title: Food production: crop plants
subtopics.summary: Glasshouses and polythene tunnels, carbon dioxide and temperature, fertilisers and pest control.

points.summary: Glasshouses and polythene tunnels raise crop yields.
Extra carbon dioxide and warmth in glasshouses increase yield.
Fertiliser increases crop yield.
Why pests are controlled, and the pros and cons of pesticides and biological control.

subtopics.title: Food production: micro-organisms and fish farming
subtopics.summary: Yeast in bread, Lactobacillus in yoghurt, industrial fermenters and fish farming.

points.summary: Yeast is used to make food such as bread.
Practical: investigate anaerobic respiration of yeast in different conditions.
Lactobacillus bacteria are used to make yoghurt.
Industrial fermenters and why aseptic conditions, nutrients, temperature, pH, oxygen and stirring are controlled.
How fish are farmed intensively: water quality, predation, disease, waste, feeding and breeding.

subtopics.title: Selective breeding and genetic modification
subtopics.summary: Selective breeding of plants and animals, restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors, GM insulin and GM crops.

points.summary: Selective breeding of plants with useful features.
Selective breeding of animals with useful features.
Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sites and ligase joins DNA.
Plasmids and viruses act as vectors carrying recombinant DNA into cells.
Making human insulin with GM bacteria grown in a fermenter.
GM crops can improve food production.
Transgenic means carrying genetic material from another species.

subtopics.title: Cloning
subtopics.summary: Micropropagation of plants and cloning mammals by nuclear transfer, and uses of cloned transgenic animals.

points.summary: Micropropagation grows explants into plants in vitro.
Micropropagation gives large numbers of identical plants with useful features.
Cloning a mammal by putting a diploid nucleus into an enucleated egg, as with Dolly the sheep.
Cloned transgenic animals can make human proteins.
